extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and students studying media, law, and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions relevant to producing or publishing satirical cartoons (especially those that might offend religious groups), covering legal, editorial, safety, diplomatic, and ethical considerations. Draws on the Danish Muhammad cartoons controversy as a case study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Danish criminal code §140
rubrics_metrics.description: See Law Proclamation no. 909 of the 27th of September 2005 §140 which was in force at the time the drawings were published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal context: whether a specific domestic criminal-code provision was in force at the time of publication may affect prosecutorial or regulatory responses to controversial cartoons. Use this when assessing past legal risk or precedent in Denmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Danish criminal code §266b (hate speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: “§ 266b of the Danish criminal code” is cited in the article as relevant legal material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to hate-speech/anti-discrimination law used to evaluate whether published material crosses legal thresholds for incitement, hatred or discrimination. Assessors should consider whether content targets a protected group and whether it meets statutory elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU standard on condoning or grossly trivialising genocide
rubrics_metrics.description: “The agreement makes it an offence to condone or grossly trivialise crimes of genocide – but only if the effect is incitement to violence or hatred.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating potentially offensive images, consider supranational criminal standards (e.g., EU measures) that criminalise condoning/trivialising genocide — but note the legal threshold depends on the effect (incitement to violence or hatred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious prohibition on depiction of prophets / images
rubrics_metrics.description: “Islam, like Judaism and Christianity, strictly prohibits idolatry... the hadith do prohibit images of any living being. As a result, many Muslims today argue that the visual depiction of the Prophet (and other prophets ... ) should not be allowed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural/religious sensitivity criterion: understand that many in the target faith view depictions of prophets as forbidden; this shapes both the anticipated reception and ethical considerations for publication. Use religious norms to anticipate offense and to inform editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial balancing of free press and respect for religious views
rubrics_metrics.description: “Editors weigh free press, respect for religious views.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial criterion: publications must balance claims of freedom of expression against respect for religious communities. The decision to publish offensive satire should consider journalistic values, audience impact, and potential harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target specificity versus blanket critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation/summary: Some commentators argued the cartoons targeted "some bestemte fundamentalistiske træk" (certain fundamentalist traits) rather than Islam as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether satire is directed at specific behaviours/ideologies (e.g., fundamentalism) versus an entire religion or group; targeting specificity affects moral and legal evaluation and may reduce or increase perceived offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship / refusal to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: References such as “Profetens ansigt: Ingen selvcensur blandt tegnere” and reporting of papers refusing certain cartoons (e.g., Jesus, Holocaust) indicate editorial choices on self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial practice criterion: whether and why a publication chooses self-censorship (refusal to publish particular images) is a salient standard. Consider consistency, precedent, and the reasons (ethical, legal, safety) for withholding material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and security considerations for cartoonists and staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple references: “Danish cartoonists fear for their lives”, attacks, death threats, attempted attacks and security incidents following publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk-management criterion: assess risks to individuals and organizations (threats, violence) arising from publication. Decisions should factor in staff safety, need for protection, and potential escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for diplomatic and international repercussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous diplomatic protests and responses (e.g., “Letter from 11 ambassadors”, government responses, diplomatic protests against the cartoons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External-relations criterion: evaluate how publication may affect diplomatic relations, prompt embassy protests, or create international incidents. Editors and policymakers should anticipate and weigh geopolitical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of inciting violence or mass protest
rubrics_metrics.description: Documented outcomes include arson, protests, demonstrations and deaths linked to the cartoons (e.g., 'Arson and Death Threats', '16 die in cartoon protests in Nigeria').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-safety/effect criterion: when judging content, consider empirical likelihood that it will provoke violent responses or mass unrest. This is distinct from offensiveness and relevant to legal and ethical risk assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual securitization: imagery's role in security framing
rubrics_metrics.description: “Visual Securitization: Taking Security Studies from the Word to the Image” is cited, indicating images can shift security discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical criterion: images can perform securitizing moves (framing actors or issues as security threats). Assess how visual choices may reframe public perception and political responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal mobilization and likely court outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple references to court decisions, prosecutions, and legal inquiries (e.g., French court clears weekly, decisions on possible criminal proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal-strategy criterion: consider precedents, jurisdictional differences, and likely legal outcomes when assessing whether to publish contentious material. Past litigation informs risk and defense strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial consistency in allowing/rejecting controversial images
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: some papers refused Jesus cartoons or Holocaust cartoons while publishing others; Yale Press decision to nix images of Muhammad is noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency criterion: evaluate whether editorial policies are applied coherently across topics and targets. Perceived hypocrisy or selective standards can influence public reaction and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-speech value: right to ridicule versus harm
rubrics_metrics.description: References and essays (e.g., 'The Right to Ridicule', 'Stand up for Denmark!') debate the legitimacy of ridicule as free expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative criterion: weigh the democratic/social value of ridicule and satire against harms (offence, social exclusion, incitement). This informs ethical justification for publishing provocative material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of political exploitation and opportunism
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary noting 'Opportunists Make Use of Cartoon Protests' and radical actors exploiting the controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political-risk criterion: assess how third parties (political groups, extremists, opportunists) might instrumentalize the controversy to advance agendas, inflame tensions or recruit. Anticipate secondary uses of published material.
